title: Reliance IPO — creating the Indian equity cult
statement: Ambani took Reliance Textiles public in 1977, marketing shares door-to-door to ordinary Indians in Gujarat — a population the broker community assumed would never buy stocks.
outcome: The issue was oversubscribed multiple times; within a decade Reliance had hundreds of thousands of shareholders and had converted middle-class India into equity investors, a constituency no listed company had before.

title: Patalganga and Hazira — betting on world-scale petrochemicals
statement: Under licence-raj constraints, Ambani built the Patalganga polyester complex and then Hazira at world scale, importing modular construction speed Indian industry had never seen.
outcome: Hazira's phased build-out gave Reliance the feedstock and intermediate base for the Jamnagar era; the projects demonstrated that Indian capital projects could be built at global speed.

title: The 1980s rights-issue engineering
statement: Ambani used a series of partially-paid rights issues and conversions to fund expansion without ceding control, structures that were legal under the era's rules but stretched their logic.
outcome: The financings funded Reliance's rise and triggered the era's fiercest regulatory and press battles; the structures were closed off by later regulation, and Ambani's record remains the reference case for promoter financial engineering.

title: The bear-cartel fight over Reliance shares
statement: When a bear cartel hammered Reliance shares in March 1982, Ambani's network of loyal retail shareholders bought the stock back en masse, cornering the bears.
outcome: The episode — 'the Reliance rescue' — became legend among the first generation of Indian retail investors and demonstrated the mobilizable loyalty of the shareholder base the IPO had created.
